page_title: Building a data team at a mid-stage startup: a short story

sources.entry: Building a data team at a mid-stage startup: a short story

summary.title: Building a data team at a mid-stage startup: a short story
summary.one_liner: A fictional, opinionated parable showing how a new head of data can grow a small startup data team from firefighting and fragmented data into a centralized-reporting, decentralized-work structure embedded with product teams.
keywords: data scientist vs data analyst roles
takeaways: Early-stage data problems are often organizational as much as technical: fragmented data, no clear mandate for the data team, and teams working around it by hiring their own analysts.
Centralize the reporting line for data people so they have managers who understand data, but decentralize their work by assigning them to product and business teams for a tighter feedback loop.
Opening SQL access to the warehouse and training other teams removes much of the 'SQL translation' burden, though it creates risks like fragile, unmaintained queries.
Make ML projects tangible by building a demo or small deployed prototype; stalled work often needs a working version that shows value and makes shipping estimable.
Plan for technical debt from dumping raw production tables into a warehouse; a derived-dataset layer will eventually be needed for stability and security.
summary.summary: The article is written as a fictional parable (the author calls it a parable) following a new head of data over a year at a mid-stage startup with a four-person data team. It narrates common early-maturity problems: poor instrumentation, fragmented systems, spreadsheet-driven business processes, unclear team mandates, and product teams ignoring A/B test results. Each section is followed by commentary explaining the organizational lessons, such as building a central warehouse quickly, opening SQL access, assigning data people to teams, and embedding data staff to replace shadow analysts. The piece is opinionated and explicitly not about the tech itself.
